summary: Matthew opens with a crafted genealogy from Abraham through David and the Babylonian exile to Jesus. The repeated chain breaks its normal grammar at Mary: Joseph is her husband, but Jesus is born ‘of her.’ Joseph then receives a dream, takes Mary into his home, and names the child Jesus. A fulfillment citation gives the chapter's second governing name, Immanuel — ‘God with us.’
whyItMatters: Before Jesus speaks, Matthew has located him inside Israel's covenant, kingship, exile, and hope. The chapter also introduces the book's characteristic techniques: numbered structure, scriptural fulfillment, meaningful names, dreams, righteousness expressed as obedient mercy, and the promise of divine presence.

context.author: The narrative is anonymous; ancient tradition attributes the Gospel to Matthew
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers expected to recognize Israel's Scriptures and genealogy conventions
context.date: Commonly dated after AD 70, often to the 80s or 90s; earlier dates are defended
context.setting: A literary genealogy from Abraham to the first-century household of Joseph and Mary
context.literaryForm: Genealogy followed by a dream-annunciation and fulfillment citation

outline.heading: The book of genesis: Abraham to David

keyVerses.text: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
keyVerses.why: The opening line names the royal and covenant lines through which Matthew will tell the story.

keyVerses.text: She shall give birth to a son. You shall name him Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.”
keyVerses.why: The child's name is interpreted as his vocation before he is born.

keyVerses.text: “Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall give birth to a son. They shall call his name Immanuel,” which is, being interpreted, “God with us.”
keyVerses.why: Presence becomes a frame around the whole Gospel, answered by 28:20.

questions.question: Why begin with ‘the book of the genealogy’ instead of a birth scene?
questions.answer: Greek biblos geneseōs can mean a record of origin or genesis and echoes the Greek wording of Genesis. Matthew wants the reader to hear both a family record and a new beginning. The genealogy is an argument: Jesus belongs to the story running through Abraham, David, exile, and promised restoration.

questions.question: Why does Matthew arrange the names as fourteen, fourteen, fourteen?
questions.answer: The genealogy is selective, as ancient genealogies often were. In Hebrew letter-number reckoning, the consonants of David's name can total fourteen, which may reinforce the royal emphasis. The structure is explicit; the precise reason is not. Matthew is shaping memory and meaning, not supplying a modern civil registry.

questions.question: What changes in the repeated grammar when the list reaches Jesus?
questions.answer: For generation after generation a man ‘became the father of’ the next person. At verse 16 the chain avoids saying Joseph fathered Jesus: Joseph is the husband of Mary, ‘of whom’ Jesus was born. The Greek relative pronoun is feminine singular, pointing to Mary. The grammar prepares the conception story without erasing Joseph's legal Davidic role.

questions.question: Why name Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and ‘her who had been Uriah's wife’?
questions.answer: Each woman carries an unusual or endangered place in Israel's story, and several are Gentiles or connected with sexual vulnerability. No single label fits all four. Together they interrupt a male-only cadence and show the messianic line moving through morally and ethnically complicated histories before Mary.

questions.question: What does ‘righteous’ tell us about Joseph?
questions.answer: Dikaios can describe someone aligned with God's will. Joseph holds law and mercy together: he will not publicly expose Mary, and when the dream reinterprets the situation he obeys. Matthew will keep returning to righteousness as enacted fidelity, not merely reputation or private innocence.

questions.question: How does the name Jesus work in two languages?
questions.answer: Greek Iēsous represents the Jewish name Joshua/Yeshua. Matthew links the name with saving: ‘you shall name him Jesus, for he will save.’ The sound connection is stronger in Hebrew or Aramaic than in Greek, so the Greek narrative explains a Semitic wordplay its readers might otherwise miss.

questions.question: Does ‘until she gave birth’ decide whether Mary later had marital relations?
questions.answer: No. The Greek expression states what was not true before the birth but does not by itself assert or deny what followed. Matthew's immediate point is Joseph's noninvolvement in the conception. Catholic and Orthodox traditions affirm Mary's perpetual virginity; many Protestants read later sibling references differently. This verse alone does not settle that debate.

glossary.def: Greek and Hebrew forms of the title ‘anointed one,’ carrying royal and other commissioned roles; not Jesus's surname.

A Hebrew name meaning ‘God with us,’ interpreted by Matthew and echoed at the Gospel's close.
